title: Rainbow Falls on the Wailuku River, Hilo, Hawaii, USA
desc: Water, sunlight and lush greenery come together at Rainbow Falls in Hilo, on Hawaii's Big Island. Here, the Wailuku River plunges 24 metres over a lava ledge, sending mist into the air as it reaches the pool below. On sunny mornings, that mist can catch the light and produce the colourful rainbows that gave the falls their name. Known in Hawaiian as Waiānuenue, meaning 'rainbow water', this striking waterfall is surrounded by tropical vegetation and has a special place in Hawaiian legend.

title: Sunset Point, Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah, USA
desc: Snow transforms Bryce Canyon National Park, blanketing the landscape in white while its fiery orange-red hoodoos rise above the snowy terrain. Seen from Sunset Point, one of the park's most famous overlooks, these fantastical shapes are part of the Claron Formation, whose limestone was deposited about 50 million years ago and later shaped by weathering and erosion. Because much of the park rises above 2,400 metres, snow can arrive as early as October. In today's image, snow clings to the canyon's ridges and spires while mist drifts across the cliffs, creating an iconic winter scene in the American Southwest.

title: Red squirrel in Cairngorms National Park, Highlands, Scotland
desc: As Britain's only native squirrel species, red squirrels thrive in Scotland's Cairngorms National Park. An important refuge, the park offers ancient Caledonian pine forests and newer conifer woodlands, with plentiful habitat and food for squirrels foraging for Scots pine seeds, nuts and other tasty morsels year-round. In today's image, a red squirrel is perched amid warm orange and yellow leaves, looking right at home as it ponders its next move in the Scottish Highlands.

title: Fiddlehead fern
desc: Today's image shows the gradual coiling of a young fiddlehead's tip, echoing the geometric patterns seen throughout nature. In maths, the Fibonacci sequence follows a similar progression, each number formed by adding the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and so on. Today is Fibonacci Day, chosen for the numbers of the date (11/23) to honour the sequence. Eventually the young fern frond shown here will unfurl as it grows, but elsewhere in the plant world, the sequence will continue to appear in the spiralling arrangements of sunflower heads, pinecones, succulents and pineapples.
main_text: The Fibonacci sequence was popularised through a 13th-century maths problem about multiplying rabbits.

title: The chapel and hermitage of Santa Justa in Cantabria, Spain
desc: Tucked into the cliffs of northern Spain's rugged coastline, the 16th-century Hermitage of Santa Justa, seen in today's image, overlooks the crashing waves of the Cantabrian Sea. Built partly into the rock and associated with relics of Saints Justa and Rufina, the small chapel eventually became a pilgrimage site, its sheltered stone walls creating a remarkable contrast with the powerful waves and rocky cliffs surrounding it.

title: Nice, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France
desc: Bathed in a sun-kissed glow, Nice is a patchwork of terracotta rooftops, historic churches and pastel façades along the French Riviera, as seen in today's image. Founded by ancient Greeks and long connected to the Italian royal House of Savoy, Nice officially became part of France in 1860. Today, that layered past remains visible throughout the coastal city in the south of France, where old-world architecture meets the blue Mediterranean waters and sunlit hills of the Côte d'Azur.

title: Diving humpback whale, Kvaløya, Troms, Northern Norway
desc: Off the coast of Kvaløya in Troms, Northern Norway, humpback whales move through the cold Arctic waters in search of a proper feast. They visit this region during the winter months, following migrating herring into the fjords. Humpbacks are famous for bubble-net feeding, a remarkable hunting technique in which whales blow rings of bubbles to corral fish before lunging upwards, open-mouthed, to catch their prey. In today's image, a humpback slips beneath the icy waves under a glowing pastel sky, capturing a moment of tranquillity in Norway's wild north.

title: The "Body of Knowledge" sculpture by Jaume Plensa at Goethe University in Frankfurt, Germany
desc: It's World Philosophy Day, when big thinkers gather to discuss life's eternal mysteries. To celebrate, today's image features the 'Body of Knowledge' sculpture at Goethe University in Frankfurt, Germany, which moulds steel letters from eight different alphabets into a human form. Spanish artist Jaume Plensa explains: 'Our body is the home of the spirit. The place in which ideas live.' On World Philosophy Day, we're all encouraged to look beyond easy answers and explore the questions that shape us, and the world around us.

title: Pair of barn owls
desc: These barn owls, bathed in evening light, are waiting for the hunt to begin. As night falls, these birds of prey swoop into action, listening for tiny movements in grasses or leaves made by mice and voles. Their heart-shaped faces help funnel sound into some of the sharpest ears in the animal kingdom. This allows them to locate their prey with pinpoint precision in the dark before swooping silently, their soft feathers muffling their approach. In autumn, young barn owls strike out to find their own territories. As the nights grow longer, you might spot them earlier in the evening, gliding over fields in search of supper.
main_text: Barn owls don't hoot; they make eerie, screeching noises, which might explain their reputation as harbingers of doom.

title: Trail of the Cedars, Glacier National Park, Montana, USA
desc: Today's image features the Trail of the Cedars, one of 1,126 kilometres of hiking trails in Glacier National Park, Montana. Its 1.4-km-long loop includes a raised boardwalk which cuts a path through western red cedars and hemlock trees. The park boasts routes for all abilities, taking in alpine lakes, wildflower meadows, mountain passes and wilderness stretching to the Canadian border.

title: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument, New Mexico, USA
desc: Incredible views and rock-solid foundations are part of the charm of these ancient dwellings, set into the cliffside in New Mexico. Nomads had long used the natural caves above Cliff Dweller Creek as temporary shelter, but it was the Native American Mogollon people who made them their home. Archaeologists believe they created dozens of rooms inside five alcoves in the 1270s and 1280s. Up to 15 families lived here at any one time, raising children, making pottery and overlooking the fertile Gila River valley where they grew crops and hunted wildlife. For reasons unknown, the Mogollon people moved on around 1300, leaving behind one of the American Southwest's most important archaeological sites.

title: Frozen azalea with red leaves
desc: As autumn's first frost sets in, ice crystals form on the leaves of evergreen shrubs, like this azalea. Long gone are the pinks, oranges and yellows of their spring blooms, but a new colourful display awaits, as their green leaves turn shades of red and purple. For the plants, the new pigments protect their leaves as temperatures drop, but for gardeners, they create a vibrant autumnal display, framed in white frost. When spring arrives, new growth will restore the shrub's green leaves and the colourful cycle begins anew.
main_text: The pigments that turn azalea leaves shades of red or purple are called anthocyanins.

title: Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong, China
desc: Welcome to Hong Kong, home to the world's largest collection of skyscrapers. Those pictured here tower above Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters allowed the island to develop as a busy trading port. Ships carrying tea, silk and other goods have passed through since the 1840s, but growth rocketed in the decades after World War II, fuelling a construction boom. With little flat land available between the harbour and the hills, developers had to build upwards, creating this distinctive skyline. In 2026, Hong Kong has 569 buildings above 150 metres high – more than any other city.

title: Sunset over the Damodar River during Chhath Puja
desc: As the Sun dips towards the horizon, the Damodar River becomes a gathering place for Chhath Puja. The four-day Hindu festival is dedicated to Surya, the Sun God, and Chhathi Maiya. Mainly observed in Bihar, Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh, as well as parts of Nepal, it is a celebration of gratitude for the Sun and its life-sustaining energy. Devotees observe fasting and gather beside rivers and other bodies of water to pray. One of the festival's most distinctive traditions is offering prayers to both the setting and rising sun, creating striking scenes as families and communities gather at the water's edge at dusk and dawn.

title: North Window, Arches National Park, Moab, Utah, USA
desc: Just north of Moab, Utah, Arches National Park is home to more than 2,000 natural sandstone arches – the densest concentration of arches in the world. Today's image, North Window, is one of the best-known formations in the park's Windows Section, where towering fins, openings and sculpted sandstone create a landscape that looks almost architectural.

title: The Atlantic Forest, Brazil
desc: The Atlantic Forest is one of the world's great biodiversity hotspots, stretching along much of Brazil's Atlantic coast and into Argentina and Paraguay. Its landscape includes tropical and subtropical forests, mangroves and coastal habitats, providing a home for around 20,000 plant species and an extraordinary variety of wildlife, including jaguars and golden lion tamarins. Much of the forest has disappeared over the centuries, but it continues to play an important role in storing carbon and providing fresh water for millions of people across the region.
main_text: The Atlantic Forest is home to around 150 million people, which is roughly a third of South America's total population.

title: Aerial view of Rose Island, The Bahamas
desc: From above, Rose Island looks like a brushstroke of green surrounded by every shade of blue. Just five kilometres east of Paradise Island in The Bahamas, this slender cay trades busy roads and city blocks for sandy shores, shallow waters and an inland lagoon. Its peaceful appearance comes with a touch of movie drama. Rose Island was used as a filming location for the 1965 James Bond adventure 'Thunderball', including the explosive destruction of the Disco Volante.

title: Historic district of Triana, Seville, Spain
desc: Cross the Guadalquivir River in Seville, the capital of Spain's Andalusia region, and the city's rhythm seems to change. On the other side lies Triana, a colourful neighbourhood where ceramics, flamenco and local traditions are woven into everyday life. Since the 19th century, the Isabel II Bridge, also known as the Triana Bridge, has connected the neighbourhood to Seville's historic centre.

title: Lanterns for Diwali in Mumbai, Maharashtra
desc: Across India, Diwali brings homes, streets and neighbourhoods to life with the warm glow of lanterns, diyas and colourful decorations. Known as the Festival of Lights, it celebrates themes of hope, new beginnings and the triumph of light over darkness. Traditions vary across the country, but for many families, the festivities include creating rangoli, performing Lakshmi Puja, exchanging sweets and gifts, and spending time with loved ones. Diwali is also associated with Lord Rama's return to Ayodhya after defeating Ravana. More than a festival, it's a time for togetherness, reflection and welcoming the year ahead with optimism.

title: A bison in the grasslands of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, North Dakota, USA
desc: Bison are among the largest land mammals in the world, capable of weighing up to 900 kilograms and reaching speeds of 65 kilometres per hour despite their massive size. Despite often being called a buffalo, the American bison is not one of the true buffaloes, which are native to Africa and Asia. Its scientific name, Bison bison, leaves little room for confusion.

title: Bamboo forest, Pīpīwai Trail, Haleakalā National Park, Maui, Hawaii, USA
desc: A volcano, a rainforest and a bamboo grove? Haleakalā National Park on Maui has all three. Spanning Maui from its 3,055-metre summit to the coast, the park protects landscapes that change dramatically with elevation, rainfall and temperature. It was established in 1916 as part of Hawaii National Park and became its own national park in 1961. The name Haleakalā translates to 'House of the Sun', reflecting the Hawaiian mo'olelo of Māui capturing the Sun to lengthen the day.

head_line: One step closer to the summit
title: Wooden stile at a stone wall, Black Crag, Lake District, England
desc: A simple wooden stile leads into one of England's most celebrated landscapes. The Lake District, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is a patchwork of shimmering lakes, rugged fells and centuries-old stone walls, all shaped by both nature and farming traditions.

title: People rowing among colourful bald cypress, Xuancheng, Anhui, China
desc: People paddle through a glowing maze of bald cypress in Xuancheng, Anhui, where autumn transforms flooded woodlands into a tapestry of amber, copper and deep rust. Known scientifically as 'Taxodium distichum', bald cypress is unusual among conifers because it sheds its soft, feathery needles each fall, turning reddish-brown before they drop.

title: Lake Braies, Fanes‑Sennes‑Braies Nature Park, Dolomites, Italy
desc: Lake Braies sits almost 1,500 metres above sea level in the Dolomites of South Tyrol, northern Italy. Surrounded by forest and the dramatic peaks of the Fanes-Sennes-Braies Nature Park, the lake is known for its striking green and blue waters. A 3.5-kilometre trail circles the shore, while traditional wooden rowing boats offer another way to take in the scenery. The lake is also a starting point for several mountain walks, including the Dolomites' famous Alta Via 1.

title: Polar bear and cubs by Hudson Bay, Manitoba, Canada
desc: These polar bears are gathering along the shores of Hudson Bay in Manitoba, Canada, waiting for sea ice to form so they can head back out to hunt seals. That annual spectacle inspired Polar Bear Week, observed during the first week of November, a celebration of the Arctic's largest land predator. Polar bears are powerful swimmers, expert hunters and remarkably adapted to life in one of Earth's harshest environments. Yet shrinking sea ice means many spend longer on land, making it harder to find food and raising the risk of encounters with people.
main_text: In a single season, a polar bear may cover more than 1,000 kilometres while searching for food and suitable ice.

title: Black Forest, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
desc: Today we're enjoying the misty views sweeping across the Black Forest, which stretches for around 160 kilometres across south-west Germany, bringing together wooded hills, deep valleys, lakes and charming towns. Its highest point, Feldberg, rises to 1,493 metres, while the Black Forest is also the starting point for the Danube and Neckar rivers. There's plenty of history and tradition here too. Forestry has long played an important role in the region, while its centuries-old clockmaking heritage helped make the distinctive cuckoo clock famous far beyond Germany.
